gaps.sentence: We were asked to ___ an experiment in the laboratory.
gaps.explanation: do an experiment is the standard collocation in scientific contexts.

gaps.sentence: She ___ a quick shower before leaving the gym.
gaps.explanation: have a shower is the standard British English collocation; 'made a shower' is wrong.

gaps.sentence: He ___ a serious accident on his motorbike last year.
gaps.explanation: have an accident is the fixed collocation for being involved in one.

gaps.sentence: The company ___ losses of two million last year.
He was sent to prison for ___ the law.
gaps.hint: collocation with 'the law' (opposite of obeying it)
gaps.explanation: break the law means to commit a crime; after the preposition 'for' the -ing form is needed.

gaps.sentence: Over five hundred athletes will ___ part in the games.
gaps.explanation: take part in something means to participate in it.

gaps.sentence: The roads were almost empty — the traffic was surprisingly ___.
gaps.explanation: light traffic means few vehicles on the road; its opposite is heavy traffic.

gaps.sentence: He ___ some ridiculous excuse about his car breaking down.
gaps.explanation: make an excuse is the fixed collocation; 'tell an excuse' is not used.
